meeting_header: Date: 2026-04-10 15:00 UTC, Duration: ~62m, Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Cho (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Celestia Head of ML), Ethan Reynolds (Platform), Priya Kapoor (Security), Noah Li (SRE)
summary: Deep technical review of prefix/prompt caching strategy focusing on hit rates, cache key design, multi-tenant safety, and interactions with batching, KV cache, quantization, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreement to run bench on private cluster and share cache-key proposal.
topics: Interaction with batching and KV cache semantics
Quantized model behavior with prefix cache
VPC / on-prem constraints and audit logs
transcript: [00:00] Samir (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Maya (Celestia): Maya here, hi Samir. Ethan and Priya on my side, and Noah just joined - hey all.
[00:15] Samir: Great. Lena from our SE team will lead the deep dive on prefix caching — I'm here to cover rollout/contract stuff. Lena over to you.

[00:22] Lena (Redwood SE): Cool, thanks. Objective today is to walk through our prefix caching strategy — hit rates, cache-key design, tenant isolation, and then align on a POC plan. I may jab into batching and quantization impacts as we go.

[00:40] Ethan (Celestia): Quick context: our usage pattern — ~120 qps peak for chat endpoint, about 40% of requests share common system prompts and customer prefixes. Latency SLO is 150ms p95; current infra is GKE with NVIDIA A10s, and we are evaluating Redwood Private on prem for sensitive data.

[01:05] Lena: Good. So prefix cache here means we store the KV cache state for repeated prefixes so we avoid re-computing the same attention keys/values for the early tokens. Works best when prompts have stable starts — system instruction + user profile. Hit rates depend on cardinality of prefix keys.
[01:28] Maya: Our main question is how to define the cache key. We have multi-tenant traffic and per-customer fine-grained personalization. We don't want leakage across tenants, obviously.

[01:40] Lena: Totally. We recommend cache keys that include: model_id, model_version, quantization_profile, prefix_hash, tenant_id, and a privacy tag. Example key: redwood::model-v2::quant-4bit::tenant-314::sha1(prefix). We can HMAC the prefix hash with a tenant-specific secret so raw prompt content isn't in the key store.
[02:05] Priya (Celestia Security): HMAC is good. Do you support KMS-backed keys per-tenant? We need to ensure key rotation and audit logs for compliance.

[02:18] Lena: For Redwood Private yes, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. Keys are tenant-scoped; rotation supported. For hosted, we provide tenant isolation and can use per-tenant encryption keys on request (enterprise). Audit logs capture cache hits/misses and key ops.
[02:38] Noah (SRE): Operationally, what about eviction and memory pressure? If we have many tenants, cache could explode.

[02:47] Lena: We have configurable TTLs and LRU policies per cache shard. For multi-tenant environments we shard by tenant or by hash ranges; we also expose quotas: max entries per tenant, soft evictions, and backpressure to reduce allocations. We also recommend prefix canonicalization to reduce variance — strip non-deterministic tokens and normalize whitespace.
[03:15] Ethan: About canonicalization — some of our prompts include user context like dynamic timestamps. How do you avoid low hit rates from ephemeral tokens?

[03:24] Lena: Two approaches: 1) normalize / remove ephemeral fields before generating a prefix key (we provide middleware examples), 2) use n-gram prefixing where we cache only the stable early tokens (e.g., first 20 tokens), not the entire user message. That increases hit rate but you pay for a slightly less precise context. Tradeoff discussion: higher hit rate reduces compute but could impact final token quality if important tokens are stripped.
[03:55] Maya: Hit-rate targets — what do you typically see? Our internal experiments show ~18% raw hit with naive keys.

[04:03] Lena: In our experience, with good canonicalization and tenant-aware keys, customers move to 30-60% hit rates for chat-like workloads where system prompt+user preface is stable. For highly personalized prompts it's lower. We'll model expected hit-rate uplift in the bench we'll run.

[04:26] Samir: Also worth noting that hit rate interacts with batching. If you have many partial matches, the runtime batching logic can collapse requests and still reduce per-token cost. Lena, can you explain interactions with continuous KV cache and batching?

[04:41] Lena: Sure. Two pieces: batch formation and KV reuse. For batching, we group requests by model and sequence-length buckets. If a request hits the prefix cache, the runtime can skip token generation for those tokens and fast-forward to the residual tokens, then join into a batch with other in-flight requests. The KV cache gives us the token-level hidden states; we still need to align positions — it's non-trivial but we handle different offsets with our runtime. There are edge cases where partial prefixes cause misalignment; we do padding and position offset meta to solve that.
[05:20] Ethan: Padding/pseudopositioning — does that add latency?

[05:24] Lena: Minimal. The overhead is a few milliseconds per request, but that is dwarfed by saved compute if the prefix is long. For your 150ms p95 SLO, it's usually a win if you have >=10 token prefix savings on GPUs like A10 or A100.
[05:40] Priya: Quantization — does 4-bit or 3-bit quantization change the cache behavior? Any correctness issues when reusing prefix KVs across quantized runs?

[05:51] Lena: Important point. We version cache entries by quantization profile (hence key includes quantization_profile). If you switch quantization of the model, cached KV encodings are not compatible. Also some quantization schemes are lossy and can slightly shift logits; we track cache quality metrics and can tie-set model quantization to cache TTLs for safety. During POC we recommend fixed quantization per variant to avoid mismatch.
[06:20] Maya: Multi-tenant safety — if we shard by tenant ID, are there risks of tenant id collisions if a tenant rotates id or if we replicate caches?

[06:30] Lena: We use stable tenant UUIDs. If a tenant rotates an external ID, the internal tenant UUID remains stable. On replication, we keep tenant prefixes namespace-isolated. Additionally, we can encrypt keys at rest and separate physical cache clusters per tenant for the highest isolation. That's an opt-in config for Dedicated/Private.
[06:50] Noah: How do you handle cache poisoning or attacker-supplied prefixes? Can a bad actor craft prefixes to force evictions?

[06:58] Lena: Rate limits and quota per tenant plus entry-size limits mitigate eviction attacks. We also support write-only access patterns and allow customers to filter out untrusted user-generated content from prefixing. For hosted mode we have guardrails; for Private you control ingress.
[07:18] Ethan: Benchmarks — can you share an example of expected latency improvement and cost reduction?

[07:24] Lena: Example from a customer with stable system prompts: 40% prefix hit, median latency improved 20-30ms and p95 improved by ~50-80ms on heavy loads; token compute cost reduced by ~35%. We'll provide a bench spreadsheet with breakdowns (tokens saved, effective throughput increase, CPU/GPU utilization).
[07:45] Samir: We'll attach a spreadsheet and the raw logs from the bench run in the next steps. Maya, you mentioned wanting the on-prem POC — what's your timeline?
[07:54] Maya: We're aiming to pick a vendor by end of April, kick off POC in May, production by July. Security signoff is gating — Priya will need encryption/KMS, audit, SOC2 evidence.
[08:06] Priya: Also need deterministic eviction behavior documented, and ability to purge a tenant's cache on demand for GDPR right-to-erasure cases.
[08:15] Lena: We support tenant-level purge APIs and purge-on-demand. We'll document purge semantics and provide retention TTL configs.
[08:25] Ethan: Operational question: where is the cache hosted in Redwood Private? Inside the customer's VPC or in the Redwood control plane?

[08:31] Lena: For Redwood Private the cache process runs in the customer's environment—inside the VPC or on-prem VM—so you maintain network control. Control plane metadata may be optional and can be disabled for high-compliance customers.
[08:45] Maya: If it's in our VPC, what about metrics and observability? We need token-level breakdowns and per-route hit rates.

[08:52] Lena: We export detailed metrics to Prometheus endpoints in customer VPCs; Console shows per-route hit rates, cache size, eviction counts, and per-tenant quotas. For hosted customers, we provide dashboards but scrubbed for tenant privacy unless requested.
[09:06] Samir: Quick aside — competitor question. You mentioned Anthropic earlier — customers ask about how we compare on deterministic caching and productionizing. Short answer?

[09:14] Lena: Our difference is runtime-level integration: KV-aware batching, tenant-scoped encryption, first-class Private/VPC deployment where cache lives in customer network and integration with KMS/HSM. We'll share a short comparison doc.
[09:30] Maya: Edge case: what if the prefix cache hits but the downstream model rollout changes behavior (e.g., we roll from v1 to v1.1) — do you automatically invalidate caches?

[09:38] Lena: Cache keys include model_version; we also provide explicit cache invalidation hooks during rollouts. You can configure automatic invalidation during rollouts or staged invalidations per tenant.
[09:50] Ethan: About cache warm-up during canary: can we pre-populate caches with golden prompts?
[09:54] Lena: Yes — you can seed caches. We offer tooling to ingest golden prompt sets to warm prefixes across nodes to avoid cold-starts.
[10:02] Priya: Audit logs — need to ensure we can link a cache hit/miss to an anonymized request id for compliance traces. Does Redwood log request ids with hits?

[10:12] Lena: We log anonymized request ids and correlation IDs. We don't store raw prompt content unless configured; correlation can be enabled in Private. Logs include hit/miss, shard id, tenant id, and cache key hash.
[10:26] Maya: One more on quantization — if we compress KV state for memory savings, does that affect correctness?

[10:33] Lena: We currently store raw float32 KV for highest fidelity in default; for memory-constrained configs we offer quantized KV encodings with explicit fallbacks. Quantized KV may slightly change outputs in edge cases; we detect output drift and surface regression alerts.
[10:49] Noah: Can we have hybrid mode — hot prefixes in-memory KV and cold prefixes on SSD-backed store?

[10:55] Lena: Yep. Tiered cache supported: an in-memory LRU plus persistent local SSD tier. Cold hits incur higher latency but avoid recompute compared to full generation. We surface latencies per tier in metrics.
[11:08] Ethan: Failure modes — if a node serving cached prefixes fails, do we lose warm state? Any replication?

[11:15] Lena: We replicate blocks across a small replication factor; warm state is replicated asynchronously. For strict durability we recommend persistent tier + replication. During failover we may re-compute prefixes briefly until replication catches up.
[11:30] Maya: For the POC, we'll need a template for cache key config, canonicalization rules, and the bench harness. Can you provide?

[11:37] Lena: Yes — action item: we'll send a cache-key design doc with examples, canonicalization tooling snippets (Python/Node), and the bench harness. We'll also include expected metrics to collect (hit-rate by prefix, token savings, latency delta p50/p95, eviction counts).

[11:55] Samir: Wrap-up time. Quick recap: Redwood to send bench spreadsheet + logs, cache-key design doc, SOC2 docs; Celestia to share prompt distributions and confirm POC timeline. Lena to prepare modeling example for hit-rates. Anything else?
[12:06] Maya: Please include purge demo and KMS integration notes. Priya: we'll review and list compliance questions to send back.
[12:14] Priya: I'll add questions on key rotation windows, HSM attestations, and purge SLAs.
[12:20] Samir: Perfect. We'll aim to have those items in the next 48-72 hours. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the POC kickoff.
[12:28] Lena: Thanks all. Bye.
[01:02:10] system: Meeting ended
